new_statements.rule_in_words: Native words are monosyllables or disyllables of the sesquisyllabic type (reduced presyllable with schwa alternating with a bare cluster, e.g. kə̆dɛn ~ kldɛn); in disyllables the first (pre-)syllable is always unstressed, so word prominence falls on the final, main syllable. The author separately notes word-level pitch patterns (rising/level/falling) but explicitly leaves register/tone undetermined.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is limited to disyllabic words (monosyllables trivially bear stress). Reduplications (ktut ktit 'rough') and two-word compounds (tat sŋăj 'sun') are treated as separate categories without a stress statement. Loanwords from Lao/Chinese not discussed prosodically.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement about lexical disyllables (presyllable + main syllable), based on the author's September 1971 fieldwork at Muong Pon, Sam Neua (Houaphan) Province, elicited through Lao; citation forms. No phrase-level prosody discussed. The tone/register question (sec. 2.5) is flagged as unresolved, so the language is described neither as clearly tonal nor as having contrastive stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bui 2000 describes the Phong spoken around Muong Pon (Houamuang district, Sam Neua = Houaphan Province), recorded in 1971; the author names subgroups Phong Phen, Phong Piet, Phong Lan. Tappe & Badenoch 2021 place Bui's variety in the 'Phaen-type' cluster (Pung, Phaen, Laan) rather than the 'Piat-type' cluster (Piat, Tapuang, Khami) to which Kaniang/Kniang belongs. Glottolog phon1246 'Phong-Kniang' / ISO pnx is the single code covering all Khmuic Phong of Houaphan, so the statement applies to the language as coded but not specifically to the Kniang (Kaneng) dialect. Not to be confused with Vietic 'Phong' (phon1243, ISO hnu) of the Pangloss Ferlus recordings, nor with the Bolikhamxai 'Phong' which Kato's KAKEN report identifies as Vietic.

sources.note: Checked and excluded: this Pangloss 'Phong' is the Vietic Hung/Phong cluster (Toum, Ly Ha, Tay Poong; Glottolog phon1243, ISO hnu), not Khmuic Phong-Kniang; untranscribed audio only.

sources.citation: Tappe, Oliver & Nathan Badenoch. 2021. Neither Kha, Tai, nor Lao: Language, Myth, Histories, and the Position of the Phong in Houaphan. Japan-ASEAN Transdisciplinary Studies Working Paper Series No. 12. Kyoto: CSEAS, Kyoto University.
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. Sec. 6 'Phong Linguistic Ethnology' compares Phong varieties (Piat, Tapuang/Cepuang, Pung, Phaen, Laan, Khami, Kaniang, Bui's Muong Pon data, Kato 2013 data) lexically/phonologically; sec. 7.1 says the Phong of Lagreze's 1925 dictionary 'clearly has a sesquisyllabic word structure, onset clusters, voiced and unvoiced stops, and finals /-l,-r,-y,-s,-h,-ʔ/'; p.21 refers to Phong speakers as 'speakers of non-tonal Austroasiatic languages'. Groups Bui's variety with the Phaen-type cluster (Pung, Phaen, Laan) as opposed to the Piat-type cluster (Piat, Tapuang, Khami).
